title: Wrestling at night (Genesis 32:22–32)
hookLine: Jacob wrestles a stranger till dawn: I won't let you go unless you bless me

cards: Twenty years have passed. Jacob is rich now, with two wives, children and flocks, and he's finally going home, toward Esau. Messengers bring news: your brother is coming to meet you, with four hundred men.

Jacob splits his camp in two, so if one half is attacked the other might escape. He sends gift after gift ahead: goats, camels, cattle, donkeys. He sends his family across the river Jabbok in the dark.
And then, in the King James Bible: "Jacob was left alone; and there wrestled a man with him until the breaking of the day." No name. No warning.

teach.h: NEITHER WINS. A HIP IS WRENCHED.
teach.b: They wrestle all night, and neither wins. The stranger touches Jacob's hip, and it's wrenched out of joint. Dawn is coming.
Let me go, says the stranger. And Jacob, limping, holding on: "I will not let thee go, except thou bless me." The stranger asks his name.
The last time Jacob was asked, his blind father said, who are you, my son? And Jacob said, I am Esau. Now he tells the truth: Jacob.
And the stranger gives him a new name: "Thy name shall be called no more Jacob, but Israel." The text gives its reason: as a prince, he has had power with God and with men, and has prevailed.
The man who grabbed blessings by trickery finally gets one by holding on, honestly, wounded, face to face. Who was the stranger? Genesis only says a man.
Jacob names the place Peniel, face of God, because he saw God face to face and lived.
The prophet Hosea calls him an angel. Some early Christian writers saw a glimpse of Christ in him. The text leaves it open.
Jacob walks away limping as the sun rises. Look at this week: Sarah's grave, chesed, a bowl of stew, the goat skins, the stairway, the wrong bride, and now this river.
A tangled family, and in Genesis, a promise that keeps hold of them anyway.

teach.h: I WILL NOT LET THEE GO, EXCEPT THOU BLESS ME.
teach.b: A whole nation will carry the name given here, to a man who wouldn't let go.

how: Many Christians turn to Jacob's wrestling when they pray through doubt or struggle, and preachers often read it as permission to bring honest questions to God; the story is also part of the weekly Torah reading in synagogues.

games.q: you're Jacob. you've wrestled a stranger all night, your hip is out of joint, and he says: let me go, the day is breaking. what do you do?
o: let go and nurse your hip.
hold on and ask for a blessing.
demand to know his name first, then let him go.
games.why: "I will not let thee go, except thou bless me." he does ask the stranger's name, but gets no answer, only a blessing and a new name: Israel.

practice: Bring up a question you usually push away, about God, or suffering, or something in your own life you can't make sense of. Don't answer it or tidy it; hold on to it the way Jacob held on, with your real name and your real feelings.
If you pray, bring it to God as it is; if you don't, stay with it a little longer than is comfortable.

wordCard.voice: Israel. The name given to Jacob at the river, which Genesis ties to striving with God and with men. It became the name of his whole family, and a people.

orig.note: Hebrew: Israel. Genesis ties the name to the verb for striving, with God and with men.

carryVoice: Your line: wrestle till the blessing. Jacob limped away with a new name. See you tomorrow.
